control_ladder.note_beginner: Once the larvae (the young, grub stage) are tunneling inside the trunk, no spray reaches them, so the fix is to go in after them by hand. In late summer or fall, scrape the soil back from the base, look for the holes marked by gum and frass (the wet, sawdust-like droppings and chewed wood the larvae push out), and run a thin, stiff wire into each hole to kill the grub. Smooth the soil back afterward. Keep mowers and string trimmers off the trunk base too, since those wounds are what draw the egg-laying moths.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: There is no rescue spray for larvae already in the inner bark, so worming is the practical home control: expose the crown in late summer or fall, locate entries by the gum and frass at and just below the soil line, and kill each larva with a stiff wire. Protecting the lower trunk from mechanical injury removes the wound sites that draw egg-laying females. Pheromone mating disruption is a commercial tool and does not scale down to a single backyard tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A spray will not reach these larvae (the young, grub stage) once they are inside the wood, so where you can get to a hole on the trunk or a main branch, dig the grub out with a stiff wire the way you would for the peachtree borer. Reach is the limit here, since this one works up in the branches rather than down at the soil line. The more lasting fix is to leave it fewer wounds to enter: clean cuts in late winter, dead or cankered bark taken off, and no torn bark or branch stubs left behind.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Worming is the only direct option and access governs how much of it you can do, because this species colonizes wounded bark on the upper trunk and scaffolds rather than at the crown. Established larvae in the inner bark sit past the reach of any spray. The durable control is denying it the wounds it colonizes: late dormant pruning with clean cuts, prompt removal of cankered wood, and no stubs or torn bark.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here, because cleanup is what lowers the beetle numbers season over season. Pick up the dropped nectarines through the summer and get rid of them, since the grub inside a fallen fruit finishes growing in the soil under the tree. On a cool early morning, while the beetles are still sluggish, spread a sheet under the branches, tap them so the beetles fall, and destroy what lands.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: clearing drops through the season denies larvae the soil development they need, and pressure falls year over year. Jarring the limbs at first light, while adults are chilled and drop readily, physically removes the beetles present now, which is the one thing cleanup alone does not do.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Kaolin clay, a fine white mineral coating you spray on, deters the beetles from feeding and laying eggs on the young fruit. Start it as the petals drop, when the damage begins, and put it back on as the fruit grows and the film wears thin.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Kaolin from petal fall is the organic deterrent this record names; it works as a barrier film, so renewal on expanding fruit is what keeps it working. University trials link heavy use to flare-ups of European red mite and San Jose scale, so hold it to the window that matters.

control_ladder.note_beginner: On a single backyard tree, this cleanup does most of the organic work. As soon as shoot tips start wilting and dying back, clip them off below the damage and destroy them, since the larva is inside; doing it early takes out the ones that would otherwise move into your nectarines later in the summer. Pull off any fruit with a gummy hole or a tunnel, and clear the drops.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Clearing infested shoots and pulling damaged fruit promptly is what a home grower has to work with. Cutting out flagged tips knocks back the early broods before the fruit-feeding generations build, and removing tunneled and dropped fruit strips out the larvae that would carry the population forward. Pheromone mating disruption is the commercial alternative and is not a fit for a single tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spraying one tree does little here, because these bugs move in from the weedy growth and brush around it. Hold a mowed strip clear of weeds around the tree instead, broadleaf weeds in particular, since that is where they build up before moving onto your fruit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Control here is habitat management rather than a spray program: the broadleaf weeds and brush surrounding the tree are the hosts these bugs breed in, and clearing them lowers how many reach the fruit. The feeding that causes catfacing happens while fruit is small, so the management window sits well ahead of the dimpling you will see at maturity.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Thrips are hard to stop once they start feeding, so for a backyard tree the plan is to cut their numbers at the source and live with some marking. Mow down or pull the weeds in flower around the tree from just ahead of bloom through it, because the thrips build up on those blossoms and move onto the opening flowers and tiny fruit. Scarred nectarines are still good to eat; peel one if the skin feels rough.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Habitat management paired with tolerance is the realistic home approach, since little can be done once feeding has scarred the skin. Clearing flowering weeds ahead of and through bloom cuts the source population that moves onto opening flowers and sizing fruit. The scarring is skin-deep, and the smooth, fuzzless skin that displays it is part of the trade for growing nectarines rather than peaches.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This is the one measure that works, and the timing decides the result. Spray fixed copper (an organic-approved copper fungicide) one time, thoroughly, on a leafless dormant tree: either in the fall once roughly 90 percent of the leaves are down, or at the end of winter with the buds still tight. Spraying after the leaves are out does not help, and leaves that have already curled cannot be undone that year, so mark the date and repeat it each season where leaf curl turns up. Copper is toxic to fish and builds up in the soil, so follow the label rate and use it sparingly.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Fixed copper is the single effective measure and the application window governs the outcome: one thorough dormant application, either in autumn after roughly 90 percent leaf drop or in late winter ahead of bud swell. The fungus infects only as buds swell in cool, wet spring weather, so a post-emergence application buys nothing and curled tissue cannot be recovered that season. Repeat it annually where the disease is established, and hold to it in mild, damp springs when risk runs highest. Copper accumulates at the soil surface and is highly toxic to aquatic life, so limit repeat use and keep runoff out of water.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cleanup is the core of this one and it runs all year. Take down and destroy the mummies, the hard shriveled fruit left over from last season, both the ones still hanging in the tree and the ones on the ground, because they hold the spores that start the next round. Through the season, pick and dispose of any nectarine you see rotting, and clear the drops and the fruit you thin off.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sanitation is the primary control because the inoculum is local and visible: mummified fruit in the canopy and on the ground carries the fungus over winter and releases spores at bloom. Stripping mummies before bud break, then removing rotting, dropped and thinned fruit through the season, cuts the spore load that seeds each new infection.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune so the canopy is open and air moves through it, since the faster the fruit dries after rain the less chance the fungus gets. Thin the young nectarines generously so that no two touch, because the rot moves straight across where skins are pressed together.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: An open canopy shortens the wetting periods that drive infection, and it earns more here than on a peach, since the fuzzless skin gives the fungus an easier entry. Thin hard enough that fruit hangs clear of its neighbors; skin-to-skin contact in a ripening cluster is a direct spread route.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the fruit as it comes ready rather than letting it hang, handle it gently so you do not bruise or nick the skin, since a wound is a way in for the rot, and get it chilled soon after picking.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Harvest on time and handle to avoid skin injury, because bruises and punctures are infection courts on a fuzzless fruit. Warm, humid conditions are what drive the rapid rot phase, so cooling promptly after picking takes the harvested fruit out of them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut out the small gummy dead patches on the twigs, called cankers, taking the cut back into clean healthy wood below the damage, and destroy what comes off. Those cankers carry spores through the winter alongside the mummies. A dip of your pruners in a 10 percent bleach solution between cuts is a sensible habit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Twig cankers, formed where blossom infections ran back into the shoot, are an overwintering reservoir alongside mummies, so cut them out beyond the visible margin into clean tissue and destroy the wood. Placing the cut far enough below the margin matters more than sterilizing, though a 10% bleach dip between cuts is still worth the moment it takes.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The variety you plant is the biggest lever here, and it counts for more on a nectarine than on a peach, because nectarines pick this up more readily. Fantasia is among the more bacterial-spot-tolerant nectarines and Hardired was bred for disease tolerance, so this is a decision to make at the nursery, before the tree goes in the ground.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cultivar susceptibility varies sharply and variety choice is the main lever on a disease with no dependable home cure, more so on nectarines than peaches. Fantasia sits toward the tolerant end and Hardired is bred for disease tolerance. The decision is made at planting and is not one you can revisit on an established tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the tree room and prune so air moves through the canopy, and keep it growing well. That does not stop the disease, but a vigorous, well-aired tree carries the damage better.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Airflow and tree vigor reduce severity rather than prevent infection. The bacterium moves in warm, wet weather, and pressure climbs where other susceptible peach and nectarine trees stand close by, so siting and canopy management lower how hard a wet season lands.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Copper is worth knowing about, but it is not a dependable answer for this one. It does more as a preventive than as a cure, and used too often it can injure the tree itself, so it will not rescue a tree that is already spotted. If you do reach for it, follow the label rate and keep it away from ponds and storm drains, since copper is toxic to fish. Treat the variety choice as the real fix.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Copper functions preventively at best, carries genuine phytotoxicity risk with repeated use, and does not cure established infection, so it is not a reliable home control here. It also accumulates at the soil surface and is highly toxic to aquatic life, which argues for limiting repeat applications. The durable answer stays with cultivar selection at planting.
